# CIS Amazon Linux 2 Benchmark v4.0.0 — coverage

**All 287 recommendations, what kind of state each one's audit reads, and whether
OverWatch can see it.**

> **On the source document.** CIS Benchmarks may not be redistributed, and the PDF is
> deliberately not in this repository. This document cites recommendation *numbers*,
> which are references, and classifies each one's audit — analysis that is this project's
> own. Unlike the sibling benchmark documents it reproduces **no recommendation titles at
> all**, not even paraphrased.

**GENERATED by `scripts/cis_al2_benchmark.py` from `engine/aws_cis_al2_map.py`. Do not
hand-edit.**

## The headline, which is not a comfortable one

This is an **operating system** benchmark and OverWatch is an **agentless control-plane
scanner**. Those two facts decide almost everything below: 252 of the 287 recommendations
read state that lives inside the instance — the contents of `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, PAM
stacks, sysctl values, file modes — and the control plane does not carry any of it.

So this document reports **35 of 287 decided**, and spends the rest of its length being
specific about why the others are not. Each blocked recommendation names the *capability*
it is waiting on rather than being filed as a backlog item, because "not built yet" and
"cannot be seen at all" are different claims and only one of them is actionable this
quarter.

## Why no checks were registered for the other 252

Registering them would have put the largest block of registered-but-unreachable checks in
this product's history into the catalogue. That is the precise failure
`docs/CHECK_FIRING.md` measures and `tests/test_unreached_modules.py` keeps at zero: a
check that is registered, counted in the published total, and cannot fire reads to every
consumer as coverage. When the filesystem extractor lands, this file is the work list —
already sorted by what each row needs.

| Source | Recommendations | Reachable today |
|---|---:|---|
| file content | 125 | none |
| file permissions | 41 | none |
| account files | 21 | none |
| running kernel | 46 | none |
| installed packages | 37 | 35 of 37 |
| systemd units | 7 | none |
| unclassified | 10 | none |
| **total** | **287** | **35** |

## What each blocked recommendation is waiting on

### `FILESYSTEM` — 199 recommendation(s)

reading a file inside the instance. The seam exists — aws_sidescan.FilesystemExtractor, fed by the EBS-snapshot block plane in aws_sidescan_ebs — but its production implementation, aws_sidescan_fs.DissectExtractor, raises SideScanUnavailable on purpose. Its own words: it NEVER returns a guessed inventory, which could false-clean a vulnerable host. Unblocking it means pinning dissect.target into the offline wheelhouse, committing golden ext4 and xfs images, and validating the parse on a Linux CI runner. That is a real project, and it lights up 243 rows here

### `RUNTIME` — 46 recommendation(s)

reading the RUNNING kernel — a live sysctl value or the loaded module list. A disk image shows what is CONFIGURED in /etc/sysctl.d, not what is in effect, and the two differ on any host somebody has run sysctl -w on. There is no read-only path to this at all: ssm:SendCommand would answer it and executes code, which is a write and outside this product's charter. Some of these rows become partially decidable once the filesystem lands, on the weaker claim of what the host is configured to do at next boot

### `SERVICE_INVENTORY` — 7 recommendation(s)

SSM Inventory reporting systemd unit state for the host. AWS:Service is collected for Windows services; whether a given Linux instance reports anything under it is not something this mapping asserts, so AL2-03 reads what is there and states it when the type is absent rather than assuming


## The checks that do fire

| Check | Severity | Decides | What it reads |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **AL2-01** | MEDIUM | 27 | SSM Inventory AWS:Application |
| **AL2-02** | MEDIUM | 8 | SSM Inventory AWS:Application |
| **AL2-03** | HIGH | 20 | SSM Inventory AWS:Service |

`AL2-00` is an INFO-only coverage statement and is deliberately not registered: it says what a host could *not* be assessed for, and an empty finding list is otherwise indistinguishable from a clean host.

## The packages and units this reads for

Package and unit NAMES are facts about the operating system rather than the benchmark's prose, which is why they appear here verbatim when its titles do not.

**Prohibited packages (27):** `autofs`, `avahi`, `bind`, `bluez`, `cups`, `dhcp`, `dnsmasq`, `dovecot`, `ftp`, `httpd`, `mcstrans`, `net-snmp`, `nfs-utils`, `openldap-clients`, `rpcbind`, `rsync`, `samba`, `squid`, `telnet`, `telnet-server`, `tftp`, `tftp-server`, `vsftpd`, `xinetd`, `xorg-x11-server-common`, `ypbind`, `ypserv`

**Required packages (8):** `aide`, `audit`, `chrony`, `firewalld`, `libpwquality`, `libselinux`, `rsyslog`, `sudo`

**Prohibited units (20):** `autofs.service`, `avahi-daemon.socket`, `bluetooth.service`, `cups.socket`, `dhcpd.service`, `dnsmasq.service`, `dovecot.socket`, `httpd.socket`, `named.service`, `nfs-server.service`, `rpcbind.socket`, `rsyncd.socket`, `smb.service`, `snmpd.service`, `squid.service`, `telnet.socket`, `tftp.socket`, `vsftpd.service`, `xinetd.service`, `ypserv.service`
